title: Tests for carbohydrates, fats and proteins
objective: Apply Molisch's test as a general test for all carbohydrates
Distinguish a reducing sugar (Fehling's-positive) from a non-reducing one such as sucrose
Apply the grease-spot and acrolein tests to detect fats
Apply the biuret and xanthoproteic tests to detect proteins, and apply all of these to identify components in real foodstuffs

theory.statement: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins each give characteristic reactions with specific reagents. Testing pure, known samples first calibrates what a positive result looks like, before the same reagents are applied to unknown foodstuff extracts.
theory.derivationNote: Molisch's test (concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates any carbohydrate to a furfural derivative, which condenses with alpha-naphthol to a violet ring) is positive for ALL carbohydrates, including non-reducing ones like sucrose — a common point of confusion, since sucrose is Fehling's-NEGATIVE (its anomeric carbons are both tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it has no free reducing aldehyde/ketone) but still Molisch-POSITIVE.
keyEquations: Carbohydrate --conc. H2SO4--> furfural derivative --alpha-naphthol--> violet ring (Molisch's test)
Peptide bonds + Cu2+ (alkaline) → violet complex (Biuret test)

apparatus.name: Biuret reagent (dilute CuSO4 + NaOH)
apparatus.why: Detects the peptide bond, characteristic of proteins

apparatus.name: Concentrated nitric acid (xanthoproteic test)
apparatus.why: Detects aromatic amino acid residues in a protein

apparatus.name: Filter paper (grease-spot test)
apparatus.why: A simple physical test for the presence of fat

procedure.text: Test pure known samples (glucose, sucrose, starch, oil, egg albumin) with the appropriate reagents first.
Add the chosen reagent and note the observation.
Note which pure samples give a positive result with each reagent, calibrating expectations.
Apply the same battery of tests to the given foodstuff extracts (milk, potato extract).
State which biomolecules are present in each foodstuff, with supporting evidence.

steps: Calibrate each reagent on pure, known samples
Apply the same reagents to the foodstuff extracts
State which biomolecules each foodstuff contains, with evidence

expectedResult.quantity: Biomolecules identified in the foodstuff extracts tested
expectedResult.statement: Sucrose is Molisch-positive but Fehling's-negative (a non-reducing sugar); starch is Molisch- and iodine-positive; oil gives a persistent grease spot; egg albumin and milk are biuret-positive (protein present). Applying the calibrated reagents to milk and potato extract correctly reveals their protein/carbohydrate/fat content.

safety: Concentrated sulphuric and nitric acids used in these tests are corrosive — handle with care, add acid to the tube down the side, not the reverse.
Discard Fehling's/Tollens'-type residues promptly as directed.
sourcesOfError: Using stale Fehling's solution (which can give a false precipitate on its own) leads to a false positive.
Mistaking sucrose's Molisch-positive, Fehling's-negative result for 'no carbohydrate present'.
Insufficient heating in the acrolein test misses the characteristic pungent smell.

viva.question: Sucrose gives a positive Molisch's test but a negative Fehling's test. Explain both results.
viva.expectedConcept: Molisch's test is positive for ANY carbohydrate, including sucrose, since it depends only on acid dehydration of the sugar skeleton. Fehling's test needs a free reducing group (a free aldehyde or an -OH adjacent to it that can tautomerise to one); in sucrose, both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond linking glucose and fructose, leaving no free reducing group.
viva.answerLogic: General vs. reducing-sugar-specific tests give different information.
viva.commonMisconception: Concluding sucrose is 'not a carbohydrate' from the Fehling's-negative result alone.

viva.question: What is the chemical basis of the biuret test for proteins?
viva.expectedConcept: In alkaline solution, Cu2+ ions form a coloured coordination complex with the nitrogen atoms of peptide bonds (the repeating -CO-NH- linkage), giving a violet/pink colour whose intensity roughly reflects the number of peptide bonds present.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the biuret test detects amino acids in general rather than the peptide linkage specifically.

viva.question: Why might a protein give only a weak xanthoproteic test despite clearly being a protein (positive biuret test)?
viva.expectedConcept: The xanthoproteic test depends on aromatic amino acid residues (tyrosine, tryptophan, phenylalanine) undergoing nitration. A protein low in these particular residues (e.g. gelatin) gives only a faint result even though the biuret test — which depends on the peptide backbone common to all proteins — is strongly positive.
viva.answerLogic: Xanthoproteic test depends on specific residues, not the general peptide backbone.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting all protein-specific tests to give equally strong results on any protein.

preLab.question: Molisch's test is positive for:
preLab.feedback: Molisch's test depends on acid dehydration of the sugar skeleton and is positive for any carbohydrate, including non-reducing sugars like sucrose.

duringLab.question: Test at least four sample/reagent combinations.

postLab.question: The biuret test detects proteins by reacting with:
options: The carboxylic acid group of amino acids
postLab.feedback: Cu2+ complexes with the nitrogen atoms of the repeating peptide (-CO-NH-) linkage.

scientificValidation.formula: Selective reagent tests for carbohydrates, fats and proteins
